lessons.title: Calculating Cost of Production per Bale or Bag
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must first know exactly what each bale or bag of silage or hay costs you to produce. This includes all your expenses from land preparation to storage. Start by listing every cost for one season. For example, if you hire a tractor to plough a one-acre field, that might cost 5,000 KES. Seeds for fodder like maize or sorghum could be 3,000 KES. Fertilizer, if used, might be 4,000 KES. Labour for planting, weeding, and harvesting: if you hire 4 workers for 10 days at 500 KES per day, that's 20,000 KES. If you rent the land, add that cost. If you use your own land, you can still estimate a rental value. Also include the cost of baling twine, plastic bags or sheeting for silage, and any preservatives like molasses. Don't forget transport to storage and any storage costs. Add all these together to get your total production cost. Then count how many bales or bags you produced. Divide total cost by number of units to get cost per unit. For example, if total cost is 50,000 KES and you produced 200 bales, your cost per bale is 250 KES. This figure is your break-even point; you must sell above it to profit. Keep records of every expense in a notebook or simple spreadsheet on your phone. Even small costs like fuel for the chaff cutter add up. If you use family labour, you should still assign a value, because that labour could have been used elsewhere. Accurate costing helps you negotiate prices and avoid selling at a loss. Review your costs each season to see where you can save, such as buying inputs in bulk or using manure instead of fertilizer. This simple calculation is the foundation of your business.

lessons.title: Setting a Profitable Selling Price
lessons.body: Once you know your cost per bale or bag, you can set a selling price that gives you a profit. But you must also consider what customers are willing to pay. Start by checking prices at local agrovets, feed stores, and from other farmers. If your cost is 250 KES per bale and others sell at 350 KES, you could price at 350-400 KES depending on quality. Your price should cover cost plus a profit margin. A common rule is to aim for at least 20-30% profit. So if cost is 250 KES, a 30% profit means selling at 325 KES. But if the market price is higher, say 400 KES, you can charge that and enjoy more profit. However, don't price too high or customers will go elsewhere. Consider the season: during dry season, fodder prices rise, so you can charge more. During harvest season, prices may drop. You can also offer discounts for bulk purchases, like 10 bales for 3,500 KES instead of 4,000 KES. This encourages large orders from dairy farmers or feedlots. For silage in bags, price per bag might be 150-200 KES depending on size and quality. Always communicate the value: your fodder is well-fermented, nutritious, and saves customers the trouble of making their own. If you deliver, you might add transport cost to the price. Be consistent with pricing so customers trust you. Keep a price list and update it as costs change. Remember, the goal is not just to sell, but to make a profit that allows you to reinvest and grow. Test different prices with different customers and see what works. Over time, you'll find the sweet spot that keeps you competitive and profitable.

lessons.title: Finding Customers: Dairy Farmers, Feedlots, and Agrovets
lessons.body: Your customers are the people who need fodder for their animals. The main groups are dairy farmers, feedlots (where cattle are fattened for meat), and agrovets (agro-veterinary shops that sell farm supplies). To find them, start locally. Visit dairy cooperatives, milk collection centres, and large dairy farms in your area. Talk to the farm manager or owner. Explain that you have quality silage or hay for sale. Leave a sample or a small bale for them to test with their cows. If cows eat it well and milk production is maintained or improved, they will buy more. For feedlots, look for places where cattle are kept in large numbers for beef. They need a lot of feed, so they can be big buyers. Agrovets are retail shops; they might buy from you in bulk and resell to farmers. Offer them a wholesale price so they can make a profit. Other customers include horse stables, goat and sheep farms, and even rabbit keepers. Use local networks: attend farmer field days, agricultural shows, and church or community meetings. Word of mouth is powerful. Ask satisfied customers to refer you. You can also use social media like WhatsApp groups for farmers, or Facebook Marketplace. Post photos of your fodder and your price. Include your phone number. For larger operations, you might contact commercial farms or even export markets, but start local. Build relationships: deliver on time, be friendly, and provide consistent quality. A dairy farmer who buys 50 bales now might buy 200 next season if you treat them well. Keep a list of customers with their contact details and purchase history. Follow up with them before the dry season when they need fodder most. Remember, finding customers is about solving their problem: they need reliable, affordable feed. If you can provide that, you'll have a steady market.

lessons.title: Packaging and Labelling for Market
lessons.body: Good packaging protects your fodder and makes it attractive to customers. For hay, you can tie bales with twine and store them under cover. But for selling, consider wrapping bales in plastic netting or storing them in a clean, dry place. For silage, packaging is critical because it must remain airtight to prevent spoilage. Use heavy-duty plastic bags or wrap bales tightly with silage film. Bags should be sealed completely. You can buy silage bags from agrovets or use strong polythene bags that are food-grade. The size should be convenient: a 50 kg bag is manageable for one person to carry. Label each bag or bale with key information: product type (e.g., maize silage), weight, production date, and your contact details. This builds trust and helps customers reorder. You can use a permanent marker or printed stickers. If you sell to agrovets, they may want your label to include nutritional information like protein content, but that requires testing. At minimum, include your farm name and phone number. For branding, choose a simple name that customers remember, like "GreenGold Silage" or "Mama's Hay". Consistent labelling makes your product look professional. You can also add a batch number for traceability. If you sell in bulk, you might not need individual labels, but you should provide an invoice with details. Packaging also affects transport: well-packaged bales stack better and are less likely to spoil. Invest in good packaging materials; it reduces losses and increases customer satisfaction. Remember, a neatly packaged product can fetch a higher price than a loose one. So take time to package properly.

lessons.title: Transporting Fodder to Markets
lessons.body: Transporting fodder can make or break your profit. You need to move bales or bags from your farm to the customer without damage or spoilage. For short distances, you can use a bicycle, motorcycle, or donkey cart. For example, a motorcycle with a trailer can carry 10-15 bales. For larger loads, hire a pickup truck or lorry. A typical pickup can carry about 50-70 bales, depending on size. Always calculate transport cost per bale. If you hire a pickup for 5,000 KES to deliver 50 bales, that's 100 KES per bale. Add this to your selling price or charge separately. If you deliver free, ensure your price covers it. For silage bags, they are heavy, so you need strong vehicles. Plan your trips to maximize load: deliver to multiple customers in one area to save fuel. Use ropes to tie down the load securely. Cover hay with a tarpaulin to protect from rain and sun, which can reduce quality. For silage, keep bags sealed during transport; avoid punctures. If you are selling at a market, you might need to rent space. But direct delivery to farms is often better because you save on market fees and reach serious buyers. Consider investing in your own transport if you sell regularly. A second-hand pickup or a three-wheeled truck (tuk-tuk) can be a good investment. Keep records of transport costs: fuel, driver, maintenance. If you use public transport, negotiate rates. Always confirm delivery times with customers to avoid spoilage. During rainy season, roads may be bad, so plan ahead. Good transport ensures your fodder arrives in good condition, which keeps customers happy and coming back.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Simple Bookkeeping
lessons.body: Record keeping is essential for any business. Without records, you won't know if you are making a profit or loss. Start with a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on your phone. Record every sale: date, customer name, quantity sold, price per unit, and total amount. Also record every expense: seeds, fertilizer, labour, packaging, transport, etc. At the end of each month, add up your total sales and total expenses. Subtract expenses from sales to get your profit. If profit is negative, you are running at a loss and need to adjust. Keep receipts for all purchases. If you don't have receipts, write down the details anyway. For sales, issue invoices or receipts to customers; this makes you look professional and helps with tracking. You can use simple accounting apps like Wave or even a notebook with columns. Separate business money from personal money. Open a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for the business. This makes it easier to track. Also keep records of your assets: baling machine, chaff cutter, etc., and their value. Record debts: who owes you money and whom you owe. Review your records weekly to catch mistakes early. At the end of the season, calculate your overall profit. Use this information to plan for next season: which costs can be reduced? Which customers buy the most? Good records also help you get loans from banks or microfinance institutions, as they want to see your financial history. Remember, bookkeeping is not just for big businesses; it's for you. It takes a few minutes a day but saves you from headaches later. Start simple and be consistent.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Fodder Quality, Moisture Testing and Safe Storage Benchmarks

This module turns the science of silage and hay into a working reference you can use at the bale, the bag and the stack. If you are selling fodder in Africa, quality is your price lever. A dairy farmer in Kiambu, a feedlot in Gauteng or an agrovet in Oyo State will pay more for fodder that is dry enough, mould-free and consistent. This lesson gives you the numbers, the tests and the thresholds to protect your margin and your reputation.

Use this module as a bench reference. Print the tables, pin the checklist in your store, and test every batch before it leaves your yard. Poor moisture control is the single biggest cause of rejected fodder consignments and mould-related losses across small and medium fodder enterprises in sub-Saharan Africa.

Why These Numbers Matter for Your Business

Every bale or bag you sell carries a hidden quality promise. If the moisture is wrong, mould develops, protein drops, and the buyer either rejects the load or pays less next season. In Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, dairy cooperatives increasingly test moisture and crude protein before accepting fodder. In South Africa and Zimbabwe, feedlots apply penalties for mouldy hay. Getting the numbers right is not academic â it is the difference between a repeat contract and a one-off sale.

The two tables below give you the reference ranges and the practical actions for each. Use them when negotiating, when training your workers, and when deciding whether a batch is sellable.

Table 1: Target Quality Benchmarks for Hay and Silage in African Markets

Parameter Hay â Target Silage â Target Business Action
Moisture content 12â18% (safe below 15%) 60â70% (baled) / 65â75% (pit) Test before baling; reject above 20% for hay
Crude protein (CP) 8â14% (legume hay higher) 7â12% (maize/grass silage) Label CP on packaging; premium for >12%
Acid detergent fibre (ADF) 30â40% 28â38% Lower ADF = higher digestibility = higher price
pH (silage only) Not applicable 3.8â4.5 (well fermented) pH above 5.0 indicates poor fermentation
Mould / visible spoilage 0% acceptable 0% acceptable Discard mouldy bales; do not blend into sale stock
Colour and smell Green, sweet hay aroma Light green-yellow, acidic smell Brown or musty = downgrade or reject

Sources: FAO (2015) Hay and Silage Making; ILRI (2013) Forage Conservation Manual; Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) fodder quality standards.

Table 2: Moisture Estimation and Drying Times by Crop and Method

Fodder Crop Method Typical Drying Time Field Test for Readiness Store As
Rhodes grass / Boma Rhodes Sun drying, turned daily 2â4 days Stem snaps, not bends Small square bales
Napier grass Chopping + sun drying 3â5 days Leaves crumble; no sap on hand Round bales or bags
Maize stover Sun drying, windrow 4â7 days Cobs dry, stalks brittle Round bales
Lucerne / Alfalfa Conditioned + sun drying 2â3 days Leaves dry, stems crack Small square bales
Maize / sorghum silage Chopping + compaction 1â2 days wilt 65â70% moisture, squeeze test Pit or bunker silo
Grass-legume silage Wilt + chop + compact 1â2 days wilt No free water when squeezed Baled silage (wrapped)

Sources: FAO (2015); ILRI (2013); University of Nairobi Department of Animal Production extension notes; South African Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD) fodder guidelines.

â  SAFETY WARNING â MOULDY FODDER AND SILAGE GAS

Never sell, feed or handle mouldy hay or silage without protection. Mouldy fodder can contain Aspergillus and Fusarium mycotoxins that cause liver damage, reduced milk yield and abortion in livestock, and respiratory disease in humans. Always wear a dust mask and gloves when handling suspect bales. Never enter a sealed silo or pit within 72 hours of opening â silage gas (nitrogen dioxide) can be fatal. Open the pit, wait 30â60 minutes, ventilate, and only then work near the face. Discard mouldy material; do not blend it into sale stock or feed it to dairy animals. If you suspect mycotoxin contamination, contact your nearest veterinary or extension officer before selling.

Practical Moisture Testing Without a Meter

Most small and medium fodder businesses in Africa cannot afford a moisture meter at every bale. Use these three field tests. They are not laboratory-grade, but they are accurate enough to protect your sale.

1. The squeeze test for silage. Take a handful of chopped forage and squeeze hard for 30 seconds. If free water drips out, the material is too wet â wilt longer. If the ball holds shape and your hand is damp but not dripping, you are in the 65â70% range. If the ball falls apart, it is below 60% and may not ferment well.

2. The twist test for hay. Take a handful of hay and twist it firmly. If it snaps cleanly, moisture is below 15% â safe to bale and stack. If it bends without breaking, moisture is above 18% â leave it in the field. If it feels cool and damp, do not bale.

3. The salt test for stored hay. Sprinkle a small amount of dry salt into a handful of hay in a jar. Shake for one minute. If salt sticks to the hay, moisture is above 20% and the batch is at risk. If the salt falls free, moisture is likely below 15%.

For commercial contracts, buy a basic moisture meter. A handheld unit costs roughly USD 40â120 in most African agro-dealer markets and pays for itself after one rejected load.

Pricing and Quality: The Link

Buyers pay for quality. In Kenya, well-made Rhodes hay with 12â14% CP and less than 15% moisture sells for a premium of 15â30% over average hay. In South Africa, feedlots pay a premium for lucerne with high leaf retention and low mould. In Nigeria, agrovets increasingly demand labelled bags with moisture and protein content. Your practical reference is also your pricing reference.

Use Table 1 to grade your batch before you quote. Grade A (moisture below 15%, CP above 12%, no mould) commands premium. Grade B (moisture 15â18%, CP 8â12%) sells at market average. Grade C (moisture above 18% or visible mould) should be reworked, downgraded or sold only for non-dairy use with full disclosure.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Test moisture before baling: hay below 18%, ideally below 15%; silage 65â70%.
  • Use the squeeze, twist and salt tests if you do not have a moisture meter.
  • Reject or rework any batch with visible mould, musty smell or brown colour.
  • Wear a dust mask and gloves when handling suspect hay or opening silage pits.
  • Never enter a sealed silo or pit within 72 hours of opening.
  • Label every bag or bale with moisture, crude protein and date of baling.
  • Grade your stock A, B or C before quoting a price to dairy farmers or feedlots.
  • Keep a batch record of moisture, weight, date and buyer for every sale.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Hay and Silage Making: A Guide for Small-Scale Farmers
  • ILRI â Forage Conservation Manual for East Africa
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation fodder resources
  • South African DALRRD â Fodder and Forage Guidelines
  • WOAH (OIE) â Animal Feed Safety and Mycotoxin Guidelines

Bottom line: Quality is your price. Test moisture, grade your batch, label honestly, and never sell mouldy fodder. The numbers in this module are your bench reference for every bale and bag that leaves your yard.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating cost of production per bale?
options: A) Divide total cost by number of bales
B) List all expenses for the season
D) Count the number of bales
quiz.explanation: You must first list all expenses to know total cost before dividing by units.

quiz.q: If total production cost is 60,000 KES and you produced 300 bales, what is the cost per bale?
quiz.explanation: 60,000 divided by 300 equals 200 KES per bale.

quiz.q: Why should you assign a value to family labour in cost calculation?
options: A) Because it is required by law
B) Because that labour could have been used elsewhere
C) To increase the cost artificially
quiz.explanation: Family labour has an opportunity cost, so it should be valued to reflect true production cost.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a production cost for silage?
quiz.explanation: Selling price is a revenue item, not a cost.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point?
options: A) The price at which you make maximum profit
quiz.explanation: Break-even point is the cost per unit; selling above it yields profit.

quiz.q: If your cost per bale is 250 KES and you want a 30% profit, what should be your selling price?
Why is it important to check competitors' prices?
options: B) To ensure your price is competitive
D) To report them to authorities
quiz.explanation: Knowing market prices helps you set a price that attracts customers while covering costs.

quiz.q: During which season can you usually charge higher prices for fodder?
quiz.explanation: In dry season, fodder is scarce, so prices tend to rise.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of offering bulk discounts?
options: A) It reduces your profit per unit but increases total sales
B) It always leads to loss
quiz.explanation: Bulk discounts encourage large orders, increasing overall revenue even if per-unit profit is lower.

quiz.q: When setting a price, what should you always ensure?
options: A) It is the lowest in the market
B) It covers cost plus profit
C) It is the same as everyone else's
quiz.explanation: The price must at least cover cost and provide a profit margin to sustain the business.

quiz.q: Which of these is a potential customer for fodder?
quiz.explanation: Dairy farmers, feedlots, and agrovets all buy fodder for resale or use.

quiz.q: Where can you find dairy farmers to sell to?
quiz.explanation: Milk collection centres are common gathering points for dairy farmers.

quiz.q: What is a good way to convince a dairy farmer to buy your silage?
options: A) Give a sample for their cows to test
quiz.explanation: A sample allows the farmer to see if cows accept the feed, building trust.

quiz.q: Why are agrovets good customers?
options: A) They buy in bulk and resell
B) They only buy small quantities
C) They never pay on time
quiz.explanation: Agrovets are retail shops that can buy large quantities to resell to farmers.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to advertise your fodder business?
options: D) Wait for customers to come
quiz.explanation: Social media and farmer groups are effective and low-cost ways to reach potential customers.

quiz.q: What should you do before the dry season to secure customers?
options: A) Follow up with previous customers
quiz.explanation: Following up reminds customers and helps you secure orders when demand is high.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of packaging silage?
options: A) To make it look pretty
B) To keep it airtight and prevent spoilage
quiz.explanation: Silage must be kept airtight to ferment properly and avoid mould.

quiz.q: What information should be on a fodder label?
options: A) Product type, weight, production date, contact
quiz.explanation: Key details help customers identify the product and reorder.

quiz.q: Why is branding important?
options: A) It makes your product memorable
B) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: A brand name helps customers remember and trust your product.

quiz.q: What type of bag is suitable for silage?
quiz.explanation: Heavy-duty, food-grade plastic is durable and safe for silage.

quiz.q: How does good packaging affect transport?
options: A) It makes bales stack better and reduces spoilage
quiz.explanation: Well-packaged bales are easier to stack and less likely to be damaged.

quiz.q: What is a common transport method for small quantities of fodder?
quiz.explanation: Bicycles and motorcycles are affordable for short distances and small loads.

quiz.q: If you hire a pickup for 5,000 KES to deliver 50 bales, what is transport cost per bale?
quiz.explanation: 5,000 divided by 50 equals 100 KES per bale.

quiz.q: Why should you cover hay during transport?
options: A) To protect from rain and sun
quiz.explanation: Rain and sun can spoil hay, reducing its quality and value.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of delivering directly to farms?
options: A) You save on market fees
D) You need to rent a stall
quiz.explanation: Direct delivery avoids market stall fees and reaches serious buyers.

quiz.q: What should you record for every sale?
quiz.explanation: Detailed records help track sales and analyze business performance.

quiz.q: Why separate business and personal money?
options: A) To easily track business profit
quiz.explanation: Separating funds makes it clear how much the business is actually making.

quiz.q: What is a simple bookkeeping tool?
quiz.explanation: A notebook or spreadsheet is accessible and effective for basic record keeping.

quiz.q: How often should you review your records?
quiz.explanation: Weekly review helps catch errors early and keeps you on top of finances.

quiz.q: Why do lenders ask for records?
options: A) To see your financial history
quiz.explanation: Records show whether your business is creditworthy and can repay loans.
